Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

SecurityEvent

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")

        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or SHA1 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or MD5 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or SHA1 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66") or MD5 in~ ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("1ab58838e5790efb22f2d35ab98c0b7d", "a7d7d6c4c3f227f7117261c63b9e23a9", "3d3a621f852c42d97fd7260681e42508", "3432dd9ac0df80ef86eb80bd080f839b", "22aaeb4946ba6d2f2e27feb7dbb295de", "f61fbfb7aa1cd5dc8f70b055b51563e2", "f169d6d172dfb775895a5e2b1540c854", "9f5f2f0fb0a7f5aa9f16b9a7b6dad89f", "28cb7b261f4eb97e8a4b3b0d32f8def1", "bae82a15d1dbfb024617b9b56a8e5f66")

AI Agent Exploits Langflow RCE to Automate Database Ransomware Attack

The Hacker News
2026-07-02 19 use cases 6 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Security firm&nbsp;Sysdig&nbsp;says it has found what it believes is the first ransomware attack run from start to finish by an AI agent. Its Threat Research Team calls the operator JADEPUFFER and says a large language model handled the whole job: breaking in, stealing credentials, moving deeper into the network, then encrypting and wiping a company's production database. Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2025-3248) via /api/v1/validate/code POST · [LLM] Langflow web service (uvicorn/gunicorn/python) spawning shell or download tool · [LLM] Nacos auth bypass (CVE-2021-29441) via 'User-Agent: Nacos-Server' to create rogue admin · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Cron/systemd persistence beaconing to JADEPUFFER C2 45.131.66.106 · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JADEPUFFER C2 beacon to 45.131.66.106:4444/beacon · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Database ransomware impact: README_RANSOM table / ransom-note strings + mass DROP · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Langflow unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2025-3248) via /api/v1/validate/code POST AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound POST requests to the Langflow code-validation endpoint that CVE-2025-3248 abuses for unauthenticated Python execution, the exact entry vector JADEPUFFER used. Article-specific because it pins the named CVE's documented vulnerable endpoint on an internet-facing Langflow box rather than a generic web exploit. Rationale: Pins CVE-2025-3248's documented vulnerable endpoint (/api/v1/validate/code) + POST, the exact unauthenticated-RCE path the article names as JADEPUFFER's way in. Defender left empty because MDE does not ingest reverse-proxy/web access logs; endpoint manifestation is covered by the execution UC. WebSearch was blocked in this session so no external corroboration could be pulled.
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.006
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow flow authors saving/validating custom Python components
  • Internal CI/CD or health-check jobs POSTing to the validate endpoint
  • Security scanners / ASM tools probing the known CVE path
  • Blue-team CVE-2025-3248 validation testing
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has "HealthCheck" and SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the request body/user-agent and source IP; confirm whether the payload contains exec/import/os/subprocess and whether the Langflow build is <1.3.0 (still vulnerable). 2) Contain: block the source IP at the WAF, take the Langflow instance off the public internet, and rotate every API key/cloud credential reachable from its environment. 3) Hunt: on the same host look for a child shell/interpreter spawned by uvicorn/gunicorn/python, beacons to 45.131.66.106, and new cron persistence.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/api/v1/validate/code"   // CVE-2025-3248 Langflow code-exec endpoint
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceProduct, DeviceVendor
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow web service (uvicorn/gunicorn/python) spawning shell or download tool AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the on-host manifestation of the Langflow RCE: the web-service process spawning a shell, curl, or wget to run recon and sweep secrets (MinIO minioadmin default, cloud keys) and reach the staging server 64.20.53.230. Article-specific because a Langflow/uvicorn parent spawning /bin/sh is the RCE payload firing, not normal app behaviour. Rationale: A public-facing Langflow/uvicorn process spawning /bin/sh or curl is the RCE detonating; enriched with the article's concrete secret-sweep artifacts (minioadmin default cred, staging IP 64.20.53.230, cloud-provider key names). WebSearch blocked so no second-source confirmation; grounded in article body.
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1059.004 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow custom components that legitimately shell out to system tools
  • In-container entrypoint scripts where python/uvicorn launches a shell at startup
  • Ops using curl/wget from an app-service context for package or model downloads
  • Health-check or exporter sidecars spawning shell probes
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("entrypoint.sh","docker-entrypoint") and FileName in~ ("sh","bash"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the child command line for recon (id, uname, env), credential paths (.aws/credentials, minioadmin), or egress to 64.20.53.230. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the Langflow process tree, and rotate all secrets that lived in that environment (OpenAI/Anthropic/DeepSeek/Gemini keys, AWS/Azure/GCP/Alibaba/Tencent creds). 3) Hunt: pivot to network events for 45.131.66.106 and 64.20.53.230, and check for a new cron job beaconing every 30 minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("uvicorn","gunicorn","python","python3","langflow","node")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| extend SecretSweep = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("minioadmin","64.20.53.230","credentials",".aws","OPENAI","ANTHROPIC","DEEPSEEK")
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("uvicorn","gunicorn","python","python3","langflow","node")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget")
| extend SecretSweep = ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("minioadmin","64.20.53.230","credentials",".aws")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, SecretSweep
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JADEPUFFER C2 beacon to 45.131.66.106:4444/beacon AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any connection to the JADEPUFFER command-and-control IP 45.131.66.106, the target of a /beacon check-in on port 4444 every 30 minutes. Article-specific: a dedicated, published malicious IP + port + URI from Sysdig's IOC list. Rationale: 45.131.66.106 is Sysdig's published JADEPUFFER C2 IP with a documented :4444/beacon check-in every 30 minutes; a dedicated malicious IP makes any hit high-fidelity. WebSearch was blocked so the IOC is taken directly from the article's Sysdig indicator list without independent second-source confirmation.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/sandbox detonation infrastructure deliberately touching the IOC
  • Blue-team IOC-validation connectivity tests
  • A benign service that later gets assigned the same recycled VPS IP (verify timeframe)
  • Security scanner sweeping the /24 that includes this IP
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process/context making the connection (ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName) and whether check-ins recur near a 30-minute cadence. 2) Contain: block 45.131.66.106 (and staging 64.20.53.230) egress at perimeter, isolate the beaconing host. 3) Hunt: on that host enumerate cron/systemd timers, look for the Langflow RCE parent-child chain, and check MySQL/Nacos hosts for README_RANSOM tables and dropped databases.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "45.131.66.106"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "45.131.66.106"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Cron/systemd persistence beaconing to JADEPUFFER C2 45.131.66.106 AIInstallation High
Hunts the persistence mechanism: a scheduled job (cron/crond/atd) launching curl/wget/shell that contacts 45.131.66.106, the article's 'scheduled task that pinged the attacker's server every 30 minutes.' Distinct from the raw network IOC because it pivots on the scheduler parent, catching the persistence even if the beacon lands intermittently. Rationale: Combines the article's 30-minute scheduled-task persistence with the concrete C2 IP 45.131.66.106, pivoting on the cron parent so the persistence is caught even between beacon hits. WebSearch blocked; IOC and behaviour taken from the article/Sysdig indicators only.
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned monitoring cron jobs that curl an external endpoint (verify the IP)
  • Admin-authored heartbeat scripts to a legitimate host that shares the /24
  • Backup/telemetry agents scheduled via cron reaching out on interval
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the cron entry (crontab -l, /etc/cron.d/*, /var/spool/cron) and confirm the target IP and 30-minute cadence. 2) Contain: remove the malicious cron/systemd unit, block 45.131.66.106 egress, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: correlate to the Langflow RCE process chain and to any MySQL/Nacos host showing README_RANSOM or dropped tables; check for a MinIO server still on minioadmin default creds.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("cron","crond","atd")
| where FileName in~ ("curl","wget","sh","bash","python","python3")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "45.131.66.106"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("cron","crond","atd")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("curl","wget","sh","bash")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "45.131.66.106"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Nacos auth bypass (CVE-2021-29441) via 'User-Agent: Nacos-Server' to create rogue admin AIExploitation High
Hunts requests to Nacos user-management endpoints carrying the User-Agent 'Nacos-Server' identity that CVE-2021-29441 abuses to bypass authentication and add an admin account, exactly what JADEPUFFER did before encrypting the config store. Article-specific: named CVE + Nacos default-signing-key takeover leading to a planted admin. Rationale: Uses CVE-2021-29441's well-known bypass signature — the spoofed 'Nacos-Server' User-Agent hitting /nacos/v1/auth/users to add an admin — which the article names as JADEPUFFER's Nacos takeover step. Defender/Falcon/Datadog empty because this is a web-request artifact those EDR/FDR feeds don't carry. WebSearch was blocked, so no external corroboration was obtained.
ATT&CKT1190 T1136.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Nacos cluster nodes using the Nacos-Server identity for inter-node calls (baseline internal peer IPs)
  • Security testing of the Nacos CVE by the blue team
  • Misconfigured client library that copies the Nacos-Server user-agent
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !startswith "10." and SourceIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external/non-cluster and check whether a new Nacos user/admin was created around that time. 2) Contain: take Nacos off the public internet, rotate the default signing key, remove rogue admin accounts, and stop it connecting to its DB as root. 3) Hunt: check the backing MySQL for a README_RANSOM table and dropped tables, and correlate with the Langflow RCE host and C2 45.131.66.106.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestClientApplication has "Nacos-Server"   // CVE-2021-29441 identity-bypass User-Agent
| where RequestURL has "/nacos/v1/auth/users"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Database ransomware impact: README_RANSOM table / ransom-note strings + mass DROP AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on JADEPUFFER's impact stage — creation of the README_RANSOM ransom table, presence of the ransom Bitcoin address / Proton contact, or a root-context mysql client issuing DROP TABLE/DROP DATABASE after the Nacos config store was encrypted. Article-specific via three unique published strings. Rationale: Three unique published IOCs — ransom table README_RANSOM, Bitcoin address 3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy, contact e78393397@proton.me — plus root-context mysql DROP make this near-zero-FP and specific to the JADEPUFFER impact stage. WebSearch was blocked so these strings are taken from the article's Sysdig indicator list without a second source.
ATT&CKT1486 T1485
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA restoring/testing on a lab copy who names a table README_RANSOM while investigating the IOC
  • Threat-hunt queries themselves logging the IOC strings into command lines
  • Legitimate scheduled DROP TABLE cleanup jobs (verify not root-from-internet and no ransom strings)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "threat-hunt" and AccountName != "dba-restore-svc"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the README_RANSOM table / note and whether DROP/TRUNCATE ran under the DB root account; identify the source session and host. 2) Contain: isolate the DB server, revoke internet exposure of the DB admin account, and preserve logs — note the actor claims AES but printed the key once and never saved it, so recovery from backups is the only path. 3) Hunt: trace back to the Nacos auth-bypass and Langflow RCE hosts, block C2 45.131.66.106 and staging 64.20.53.230, and audit MinIO for the minioadmin default login.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
    or (FileName in~ ("mysql","mysqladmin") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DROP TABLE","DROP DATABASE","TRUNCATE"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("README_RANSOM","3J98t1WpEZ73CNmQviecrnyiWrnqRhWNLy","e78393397@proton.me")
    or (SyslogMessage has_all ("DROP","TABLE") and SyslogMessage has "root")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, ProcessName, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1555.003

logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High

ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-3248", "CVE-2021-29441")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host

| order by files desc

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Long-lived cryptomining C2 (stratum) from SYSTEM context on servers / domain controllers AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the article's four-year-old cryptomining case study: unsigned miners running as SYSTEM on servers/DCs beaconing to mining pools over stratum/getwork ports for weeks or longer. Focuses on persistent SYSTEM-context egress to pool infrastructure rather than a single connection. Rationale: Anchored on the explicit 'four-year-old crypto mining activity on domain controllers' case study; stratum pool ports + SYSTEM/machine-account context + >7-day persistence is the high-fidelity combination the article says endpoint tools missed. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1496/
ATT&CKT1496 T1569.002 T1547.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain/validator node software on a lab server
  • Approved GPU-render or scientific-compute jobs using pool-like ports
  • Security tools port-scanning internal ranges hitting these ports
  • Monitoring agents polling on 5555/7777 for app telemetry
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating binary path/signature and whether the host is a DC or server; pull FirstSeen — multi-week SYSTEM egress on a DC is near-certain TP. 2) Contain: isolate host, kill the miner process, and capture the scheduled task/service/Run-key that relaunches it before removal. 3) Hunt: pivot on the pool IP/domain across all hosts, review the same persistence mechanism enterprise-wide, and check DC event logs for the original install time (may predate current retention).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemotePort in (3333,4444,5555,7777,14433,14444,45700,45560)
     or RemoteUrl has_any ("stratum","xmr","monero","minexmr","nanopool","supportxmr","miningpool","pool.min")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("system","local service","network service") or InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort), Dsts=make_set(RemoteIP) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where datetime_diff('day', LastSeen, FirstSeen) >= 7   // persistence beyond a week = the miner-on-DC pattern
| order by FirstSeen asc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstPortNumber in (3333,4444,5555,7777,14433,14444,45700,45560)
     or Url has_any ("stratum","xmr","monero","minexmr","nanopool","supportxmr","miningpool")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Conns=count(), Ports=make_set(DstPortNumber), Dsts=make_set(DstIpAddr) by DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcUsername
| where datetime_diff('day', LastSeen, FirstSeen) >= 7
| order by FirstSeen asc

PurpleFox in-memory install: msiexec.exe fetching a remote MSI AIExploitation High
Hunts the article's in-memory PurpleFox case study. PurpleFox uses msiexec.exe to download and execute its remote MSI stage (often with a randomized/.moe/.png extension), then injects via PowerShell and hides with a rootkit. Catches the on-disk pivot the fileless payload cannot avoid: msiexec reaching out to a URL. Rationale: PurpleFox is named in the article as an in-memory infection that evaded endpoint protection; external write-ups (Trend Micro, AhnLab) confirm msiexec-fetches-remote-MSI as its signature install step — a reliable on-disk pivot for an otherwise fileless chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/19/i/purple-fox-fileless-malware-with-rookit-component-delivered-by-rig-exploit-kit-now-abuses-powershell.html • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/55492/
ATT&CKT1218.007 T1055 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise software deployment tools staging MSIs from an internal HTTP repo
  • SCCM/Intune app installs pointing at an internal distribution URL
  • Vendor installers that chain a web-hosted MSI
  • Admin manually installing from a trusted download link
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sccm","configmgr","intune") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","tiworker.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the URL host and MSI reputation; internal repo = likely benign, unknown external host = escalate. Check for a child powershell.exe or wmiprvse injection within 60s. 2) Contain: isolate host, block the URL/host at proxy, and snapshot memory before reboot (rootkit hides on-disk artifacts). 3) Hunt: search for the same URL/MSI hash org-wide, look for hidden Run keys and driver services (rootkit persistence), and review SMB auth failures indicating worm-style spread.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "msiexec.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (" /i"," -i","/q",".moe",".msi",".png")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "msiexec.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

LionTail IIS backdoor: unexpected DLL written to / loaded by an IIS worker (w3wp) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the in-memory LionTail case study on critical Windows servers. LionTail (Scarred Manticore) installs as a DLL via search-order hijacking into IIS/web-server processes and talks to http.sys directly. Surfaces non-standard DLLs dropped into web dirs or loaded by w3wp.exe from outside the OS/inetsrv trees. Rationale: LionTail is named as an in-memory infection on critical Windows servers; Check Point/SecurityWeek confirm its install-as-DLL-into-IIS-via-search-order-hijacking + http.sys behavior, so DLLs appearing in inetpub/inetsrv or loaded by w3wp from odd paths is the article-specific pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2023/from-albania-to-the-middle-east-the-scarred-manticore-is-listening/ • https://www.securityweek.com/iranian-cyber-spies-use-liontail-malware-in-latest-attacks/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web-app deployment copying custom .NET assemblies into inetpub
  • IIS module/extension installs (URL Rewrite, ARR) dropping DLLs
  • Developer publishing a site directly to the server
  • AV/EDR agents loading their own DLLs into w3wp for inspection
Response runbook
1) Triage: check the DLL's signer, hash reputation, and export table; an unsigned, unknown DLL loaded by w3.exe on an internet-facing server is high-priority. 2) Contain: isolate the server, capture a memory image (LionTail is memory-resident), and preserve IIS logs before remediation. 3) Hunt: enumerate http.sys URL ACLs (netsh http show urlacl) for rogue prefixes, review IIS access logs for the backdoor's configured URL paths, and check other web servers for the same DLL name/hash.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName endswith ".dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\" and FolderPath !has @"\inetsrv\" and FolderPath !has @"\Microsoft.NET\" and FolderPath !has @"\assembly\" and FolderPath !has @"\Temporary ASP.NET Files\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ModulePath=FolderPath, ModuleName=FileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\inetpub\", @"\inetsrv\")
| where TargetFileName endswith ".dll"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","trustedinstaller.exe","tiworker.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256

Web-server process (w3wp/httpd) spawning a command shell or LOLBin AIInstallation High
Hunts two article findings at once: web shells restored from backups (40% of discovered web shells lived in backups) and LionTail-style remote command execution. Web-server worker processes spawning cmd/powershell/net/whoami is the canonical web-shell / server-backdoor command-exec signal. Rationale: Directly targets the article's web-shell-in-backups finding and LionTail remote-command execution; a web worker spawning cmd/powershell/net has near-zero legitimate cause and re-fires the moment a backdoored backup is restored. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1505/003/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Web app legitimately shelling out to a build/deploy script
  • Monitoring plugins that call whoami/systeminfo for health checks
  • Custom .NET app using System.Diagnostics.Process to run net.exe
  • Admin troubleshooting an app pool via an interactive shell under the IIS account
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","\\deploy\\","msdeploy") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the child command line for recon/tasking (whoami, net user, download cmdlets); pull the web access logs around the timestamp for the requesting IP and URL/aspx/php path. 2) Contain: quarantine the web-shell file, isolate the host, and revoke the app-pool identity's cached tickets. 3) Hunt: scan web roots AND backup images for aspx/aspx/php/jsp files with recent write times or eval/exec patterns (the 40% that hide in backups), and block the source IP.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","php-cgi.exe","tomcat.exe","tomcat9.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","systeminfo.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, ChildProcess=FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","php-cgi.exe","tomcat.exe","tomcat9.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","systeminfo.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","php-cgi.exe","tomcat.exe","tomcat9.exe") Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","systeminfo.exe") by Endpoint.Processes.dest, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | sort - firstTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name IN ("w3wp.exe","httpd.exe","nginx.exe","php-cgi.exe","tomcat.exe","tomcat9.exe") Endpoint.Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","rundll32.exe","systeminfo.exe") by Endpoint.Processes.dest, Endpoint.Processes.parent_process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | sort - firstTime
Mass execution of binaries from SYSVOL/NETLOGON (abused GPO software distribution) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the 'overly permissive GPO-based software distribution' case study. Detects executables/scripts launched directly from the replicated SYSVOL/NETLOGON share across many domain members near-simultaneously — the fingerprint of malware pushed via a tampered logon/startup GPO script. Rationale: Directly grounded in the GPO-distribution case study; legitimate GPO logon scripts run from SYSVOL but a NEW unsigned binary executing from SYSVOL across 5+ hosts is exactly the 'goes wrong' scenario, and the cross-host count separates a real push from a one-off. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1484/001/
ATT&CKT1484.001 T1570
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate, approved logon/startup scripts running an installer from SYSVOL
  • A sanctioned software rollout that was genuinely pushed via GPO
  • Login scripts calling cscript/wscript for drive mapping
  • Admin testing a new GPO script across a pilot OU
Suppression filter
| where not (SHA256 in (dynamic([])) )
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the binary/script and its SHA256; verify against approved GPO scripts and check the file's signer and SYSVOL write time. 2) Contain: pull the offending file from SYSVOL, disable/edit the GPO delivering it, and force gpupdate to stop further spread. 3) Hunt: review DC Directory Service and File Replication logs for who modified the GPO script, check gPCFileSysPath ACLs for over-permissive write rights, and sweep endpoints that already executed it.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has @"\SYSVOL\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\SYSVOL\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" or FolderPath has @"\NETLOGON\"
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","cmd.exe")
| summarize Hosts=dcount(DeviceName), HostList=make_set(DeviceName, 25), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 5) by FileName, SHA256, FolderPath
| where Hosts >= 5   // 5+ domain members running the same SYSVOL-sourced binary = mass GPO push
| order by Hosts desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has @"\SYSVOL\" or CommandLine has @"\SYSVOL\" or CommandLine has @"\NETLOGON\" or NewProcessName has @"\NETLOGON\"
| summarize HostCount=dcount(Computer), Hosts=make_set(Computer, 25), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by NewProcessName, CommandLine
| where HostCount >= 5
| order by HostCount desc
title: Process Executed From SYSVOL or NETLOGON Share
id: 4a1e2f90-3c7b-4d61-9a2e-77c1b5d9a005
description: Binary or script executed directly from the replicated SYSVOL/NETLOGON share, matching abused GPO software distribution
references:

level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@Image:(*\SYSVOL\* OR *\sysvol\* OR *\NETLOGON\* OR *\netlogon\*) OR @CommandLine:(*\SYSVOL\* OR *\sysvol\* OR *\NETLOGON\* OR *\netlogon\*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\(SYSVOL|NETLOGON)\\/i OR CommandLine=/\\(SYSVOL|NETLOGON)\\/i)
| groupBy([ImageFileName, SHA256HashData], function=count(field=aid, distinct=true, as=host_count))
| host_count >= 5
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Endpoint.Processes.dest) as hosts dc(Endpoint.Processes.dest) as host_count min(_time) as firstTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Endpoint.Processes.process_path="*\\SYSVOL\\*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*\\SYSVOL\\*" OR Endpoint.Processes.process="*\\NETLOGON\\*") by Endpoint.Processes.process_name, Endpoint.Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Endpoint.Processes)` | where host_count >= 5 | sort - host_count
Remote management tool executing from a non-install (temp/download) path AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the article's 'legitimate yet suspicious' RMM finding — RMM tools appeared in every engagement that led to a detection. Flags known RMM agents launched from temp/download/ProgramData/public paths rather than their normal Program Files install location, indicating attacker-dropped remote access. Rationale: Grounded in the article's finding that RMM tools appeared in every incident-producing engagement; scoping to execution from temp/download/public paths (not Program Files) turns an otherwise-noisy RMM inventory into a high-fidelity attacker-dropped-RMM signal. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Help-desk running a portable AnyDesk/TeamViewer from Downloads for one-off support
  • MSP agent (Atera/Syncro) legitimately staging in ProgramData
  • User self-installing RustDesk from their Downloads folder
  • Portable RMM binary in a software-testing sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe") and FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the RMM tool is sanctioned for this host/user; check the incoming connection ID/email in the RMM client and the parent process that launched it. 2) Contain: if unauthorized, kill the agent, block its cloud endpoints at the proxy, and isolate the host. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same RMM binary across the estate, review outbound connections to the vendor's relay infrastructure, and correlate with new local accounts or scheduled tasks created around the same time.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("anydesk.exe","teamviewer.exe","screenconnect.clientservice.exe","atera_agent.exe","ateraagent.exe","splashtop.exe","strwinclt.exe","rustdesk.exe","meshagent.exe","netsupport.exe","client32.exe","dwagent.exe","logmein.exe","gotoassist.exe","supremo.exe","syncro.exe")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Temp\", @"\Downloads\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\", @"\AppData\")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("anydesk.exe","teamviewer.exe","screenconnect.clientservice.exe","atera_agent.exe","ateraagent.exe","splashtop.exe","strwinclt.exe","rustdesk.exe","meshagent.exe","netsupport.exe","client32.exe","dwagent.exe","logmein.exe","gotoassist.exe","supremo.exe","syncro.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\Temp\\","\\Downloads\\","\\ProgramData\\","\\Users\\Public\\","\\AppData\\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'

            - '\svchost.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

FortiClient EMS exploit chain (CVE-2026-35616) deploying EKZ Infostealer via fortitray/ipsec → PowerShell AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2026-35616 post-exploitation chain where a compromised FortiClient EMS drives the client processes fortitray.exe/ipsec.exe to spawn cmd/PowerShell that stages a CMD script under the FortiClient Trace logs and launches the fake 'FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe' patch payload. Article-specific because Fortinet client binaries never legitimately spawn shells or run a payload named FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE-2026-35616 process tree confirmed by Arctic Wolf (fortitray.exe/ipsec.exe → cmd → powershell → FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe) plus the unique CMD staging path C:\Program Files\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\{GUID}.cmd. Fortinet client binaries spawning shells is inherently anomalous, making this very high fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/hackers-exploit-forticlient-ems-flaw-to-push-infostealer-malware/
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate FortiClient auto-update writing scripts to the Trace\scripts directory during a genuine patch cycle
  • Administrator manually running cmd/PowerShell diagnostics while FortiClient tray is the foreground process (rare parent attribution)
  • EDR/AV response tooling quarantining a file named similarly to the payload
  • Security team detonating the sample in a sandbox for analysis
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("FortiClient\\FortiSSLVPNclient","FortiUpdate") and not(ProcessCommandLine has "FortiEndpoint_Patch"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm fortitray.exe/ipsec.exe → cmd → powershell parentage and whether FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe (SHA256 0da123adf9...) executed; decode any base64 PowerShell in InitiatingProcessCommandLine. 2) Contain: isolate the endpoint, kill the payload process, block hash 0da123adf9... and IP 83.138.53.110, and take the FortiClient EMS server offline for patching (CVE-2026-35616). 3) Hunt: sweep all EMS-managed endpoints for the same parent chain, the Trace\scripts drop, C:\ProgramData\log.txt, and outbound traffic to 83.138.53.110.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("fortitray.exe","ipsec.exe") and FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe"))
    or FileName =~ "FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (ParentProcessName has_any ("fortitray.exe","ipsec.exe") and NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe"))
    or NewProcessName has "FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe"
    or CommandLine has @"\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: FortiClient EMS Exploit Chain Deploying EKZ Infostealer (CVE-2026-35616)
id: 6b1f2a44-4d31-4d2e-9f0c-2a1e8c7b9d01
description: Detects FortiClient client binaries spawning a shell or the fake FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe payload, consistent with CVE-2026-35616 exploitation delivering EKZ Infostealer.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fortibleed-credential-theft-linked-to.html
  - https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/02
tags:
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent_shell:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\fortitray.exe'
      - '\ipsec.exe'
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
  payload:
    Image|endswith: '\FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe'
  staging:
    CommandLine|contains: '\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\'
  condition: parent_shell or payload or staging
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@ParentImage:(*\fortitray.exe OR *\Fortitray.exe OR *\ipsec.exe OR *\IPSec.exe) AND @Image:(*\cmd.exe OR *\Cmd.exe OR *\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe)) OR @Image:(*\FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe OR *\fortiendpoint_patch.exe) OR @CommandLine:*\Fortinet\FortiClient\logs\Trace\scripts\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ParentBaseFileName=/(fortitray|ipsec)\.exe$/i ImageFileName=/(cmd|powershell)\.exe$/i) OR ImageFileName=/FortiEndpoint_Patch\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/\\Fortinet\\FortiClient\\logs\\Trace\\scripts\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

EKZ Infostealer C2 download and HTTP-POST exfiltration to 83.138.53.110 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts network egress to the FortiBleed/EKZ C2 host 83.138.53.110, including the payload pull at /dl/p.exe and credential exfil POST to /service/save.php. Article-specific because these exact URI paths and the C2 IP are tied to the EKZ Infostealer campaign, not a generic beacon template. Rationale: 83.138.53.110 with URIs /dl/p.exe and /service/save.php is the confirmed EKZ download+exfil endpoint (Arctic Wolf). The two additional IPs are article-listed FortiBleed infrastructure (likely Tor exits — hence lower confidence on those two), so the primary alert weight is on the second-source-confirmed 83.138.53.110. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.darkreading.com/cyberattacks-data-breaches/fortibleed-attackers-firewalls-credentials-stealers
ATT&CKT1105 T1041 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or research hosts intentionally connecting to 83.138.53.110 for sample retrieval
  • Tor exit nodes 185.220.101.15 / 192.42.116.14 being contacted for legitimate Tor usage in the environment
  • Security scanners/crawlers touching the C2 IP during internet-wide scans
  • Sinkhole or takedown infrastructure now resolving to the same IP
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Windows Defender Advanced Threat Protection\")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the InitiatingProcessFileName driving the connection — powershell.exe or FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe reaching 83.138.53.110 confirms EKZ; check for the /service/save.php POST indicating data left the host. 2) Contain: block 83.138.53.110 at proxy/firewall, isolate the host, and treat any credentials on it (especially browser-stored) as compromised → force password resets. 3) Hunt: pivot on all hosts that resolved/connected to the IP, correlate with FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe execution and C:\ProgramData\log.txt creation to scope the intrusion.

| where RemoteIP in ("83.138.53.110","185.220.101.15","192.42.116.14")
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("/dl/p.exe","/service/save.php")

| order by Timestamp desc

EKZ Infostealer browser credential theft and staging to C:\ProgramData\log.txt AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts EKZ Infostealer credential collection: a non-browser process touching Chrome 'Local State'/'Login Data' and Firefox key4.db/logins.json/cookies.sqlite, plus creation of the exact exfil staging file C:\ProgramData\log.txt. Article-specific because the staging path and the FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe/PowerShell writer tie directly to the EKZ chain. Rationale: C:\ProgramData\log.txt is the exact EKZ staging file Arctic Wolf documented, and the browser secret stores (Chrome Local State/Login Data, Firefox key4.db/logins.json/cookies.sqlite) are the confirmed harvesting targets. Binding the file writes to the FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe/PowerShell writer keeps this tight to the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://www.helpnetsecurity.com/2026/05/29/forticlient-ems-vulnerability-infostealer/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/sync software copying browser profile databases (key4.db, Login Data)
  • Browser-migration or password-manager import tools accessing Login Data / logins.json
  • A benign application coincidentally writing C:\ProgramData\log.txt (common generic log filename)
  • Endpoint DLP or forensic collection agents reading browser credential stores
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","OneDrive.exe","Dropbox.exe","backup.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\Application\", @"\Mozilla Firefox\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writer of C:\ProgramData\log.txt is FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe/PowerShell (not a legit app) and check whether browser secret stores were touched in the same session. 2) Contain: isolate host, capture C:\ProgramData\log.txt for scoping, and force-reset all browser-saved and SSO credentials for the user (assume cookies/session tokens stolen → revoke sessions). 3) Hunt: look for the follow-on POST to 83.138.53.110/service/save.php and repeat the file-staging query org-wide across EMS-managed endpoints.
DeviceFileEvents

| where (FolderPath =~ @"C:\ProgramData\log.txt" and ActionType == "FileCreated")
    or (FileName in~ ("key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Login Data","Local State")
        and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe","p.exe","powershell.exe"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent

| where (TargetFilePath =~ @"C:\ProgramData\log.txt" and EventType == "FileCreated")
    or (TargetFileName in~ ("key4.db","logins.json","cookies.sqlite","Login Data","Local State")
        and ActingProcessName has_any ("FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe","p.exe","powershell.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EKZ Infostealer / FortiBleed known-bad file hash execution sweep AIInstallation Medium
Retrospective IOC sweep for execution or on-disk presence of the EKZ Infostealer payload by the exact SHA256/SHA1/MD5 published for the FortiBleed campaign. Article-specific: these are the concrete hashes tied to the fake FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe / p.exe payload. Rationale: Direct IOC match on the published EKZ payload hashes. SHA256 0da123adf9..., SHA1 17e771..., and MD5 338662... are second-source confirmed by Arctic Wolf as the FortiEndpoint_Patch.exe payload; the remaining four SHA256 are article-listed campaign samples included for retro sweep. Hash matches are effectively zero-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://arcticwolf.com/resources/blog/forticlient-ems-exploited-via-cve-2026-35616-to-deliver-ekz-infostealer-disguised-as-a-fortinet-patch/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/forticlient-code-execution-vulnerability/
ATT&CKT1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A malware analyst intentionally detonating the sample in a managed environment
  • Hash collision is not realistic for SHA256 — near-zero false positives
  • EDR quarantine copy of the file being re-scanned and matching the hash
  • Threat-intel enrichment pipeline re-hashing a stored artifact
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the match host and whether it was process execution (active infection) vs. a dormant file drop; capture full path and initiating command line. 2) Contain: isolate host, block all listed hashes in EDR, and quarantine the artifact; assume EKZ ran → treat local credentials as compromised. 3) Hunt: expand to the process-tree, C2 (83.138.53.110), and staging-file detections; check the FortiClient EMS server for CVE-2026-35616 exploitation as the entry point.

    | extend Evt="ProcessCreated", Cmd=ProcessCommandLine),
  (DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)

    | extend Evt=ActionType, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Evt, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, SHA1, MD5, Cmd
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in~ ("0da123adf9251957a4b850a3f6bd6a753dd4892be176a84a18450e899534cc5e","d91c00fad521e76efa89715cca89db487d5676f2c767c883482f9c8f82bd383a","fd65051c61a904a304919c04a8c8633c001183ac73ac461cd4d9057946f02bf5","2927bc31b4f8254c6b332fc03110a6373cad00ffa2ff9de427c26bb222017bb2","2f25ea1b622abf3212141af932c2ec4cbd6b2b5903c2a531121f691227d98cff")
