title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Ghost cache-poisoning via unauthenticated x-ghost-preview header (CVE-2026-53943) AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests carrying the `x-ghost-preview` header hitting a Ghost frontend behind a shared cache (Fastly/Cloudflare/nginx proxy_cache). An unauthenticated attacker uses this header to alter the rendered response, which the shared cache then stores and serves to other visitors — enabling reflected/stored XSS and, on same-domain admin deployments, staff-account takeover. Rationale: The `x-ghost-preview` request header is the exact, article-named injection vector for CVE-2026-53943 and is not a benign header any normal browser or bot emits — its presence in inbound edge/WAF logs is a near-zero-FP signal. Splunk uses TERM() to match the header token in raw web events (headers are not first-class CIM Web fields); Sentinel searches the CEF Message/RequestContext where WAFs surface matched request headers. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-62q6-4hv4-vjrw • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-53943
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.007
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ghost's own preview/staging workflow where an authenticated editor legitimately requests preview content (the header is used as designed) — distinguishable by an accompanying valid admin session cookie/authenticated source IP
  • Security-scanning tools (Burp, Nuclei, internal DAST) firing the CVE-2026-53943 test payload during an authorized assessment
  • Synthetic-monitoring or QA scripts that replay saved requests including custom headers
  • A misconfigured internal proxy that unconditionally forwards/injects a preview header on all upstream requests
Suppression filter
| where not (RequestClientApplication has_any ("Burp","Nuclei","HealthCheck","pingdom","StatusCake") or SourceIP in ("127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the target host runs Ghost <= v6.36.0 and whether frontend and admin share the same domain (same-domain = staff-takeover exposure). Check whether the shared cache stored the response (look for a subsequent cache-HIT on the same URL/varied output) and identify the source IP + user-agent. 2) CONTAIN: At the caching layer, add a rule to bypass/deny cache for any request bearing `x-ghost-preview`; purge the affected cache keys/URLs. Upgrade Ghost to v6.37.0+. If same-domain admin and poisoning is confirmed, use Settings > Danger Zone > 'Reset all authentication' (Ghost v6.41.0+) to invalidate staff sessions. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the source IP for other header-injection or preview-abuse attempts; review admin/staff sign-ins and session activity after the poisoning window for signs of account takeover; check edge logs for other cached poisoned URLs served to third parties.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DeviceVendor in~ ("Fastly","Cloudflare","NGINX","Imperva","F5","Akamai") or DeviceProduct has_any ("WAF","proxy","cache")
| where Message has "x-ghost-preview" or RequestContext has "x-ghost-preview"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fleet valuesFrom cross-namespace secret/configmap reference (CVE-2026-44935) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts Rancher Fleet GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle custom resources whose spec contains a `valuesFrom` block with a secretKeyRef/configMapKeyRef, the exact mechanism CVE-2026-44935 abuses to read secrets in namespaces the tenant is not authorized for. Article-specific because it pivots on the Fleet CRD resource names plus the `valuesFrom` key-reference structure rather than generic secret access. Rationale: Uses the exact Fleet CRD resource names (gitrepos/helmops/bundles from go:github.com/rancher/fleet) and the `valuesFrom` + secretKeyRef/configMapKeyRef structure named in GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x as the exploitation vector; high-fidelity because legitimate fleet.yaml normally references secrets in the same namespace only. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/007/
ATT&CKT1552.007
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate multi-namespace GitOps deployment where an operator intentionally references a shared config namespace
  • Fleet platform team testing valuesFrom against a sanctioned central secrets namespace
  • CI pipelines that template Bundles with valuesFrom to a common values ConfigMap
  • Upgrade migrations that recreate existing GitRepo resources with unchanged valuesFrom blocks
Suppression filter
| where not (Username has "system:serviceaccount:cattle-fleet-system" and ObjNamespace == extract(@"namespace:\s*([a-z0-9-]+)", 1, ReqStr))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RequestObject; compare the namespace inside valuesFrom to ObjectRef.namespace and to the tenant that owns the requesting Username — a mismatch to a namespace the tenant has no RBAC in is the true positive. 2) Contain: delete/suspend the offending GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle, and rotate any secret whose name/namespace/key appears in the valuesFrom reference (advisory explicitly recommends rotation). 3) Hunt: enumerate all Fleet CRs created by the same Username across the cluster and check whether the Fleet agent service account subsequently read those referenced secrets (see companion fan-out UC).
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| extend ObjResource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), ObjNamespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)
| where ObjResource in ("gitrepos","helmops","bundles")
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has "valuesFrom" and (ReqStr has "secretKeyRef" or ReqStr has "configMapKeyRef")
| where ReqStr has "namespace"    // cross-namespace ref requires an explicit namespace inside valuesFrom
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, ObjResource, ObjNamespace, RequestUri, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fleet agent service account reads secrets across multiple namespaces (CVE-2026-44935) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the downstream-cluster fingerprint of CVE-2026-44935: the Fleet agent service account issuing get/list of secrets or configmaps across an abnormal number of distinct namespaces within a short window, indicating cross-tenant credential harvesting via unrestricted valuesFrom/HelmOp deployment. Article-specific because it keys on the Fleet agent SA identity and the cross-namespace fan-out the advisory tells defenders to review logs for. Rationale: Pivots on the Fleet agent service account identity (cattle-fleet-system fleet-agent) reading secrets/configmaps across namespaces — the exact post-exploit behaviour GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x tells operators to review cluster logs for and to drive credential rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr65-5cpm-g36x • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/007/

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment

  • Backup/DR tooling running under a fleet-labelled SA enumerating secrets
  • Cluster-wide chart rollout (e.g. cert-manager, monitoring) driven through Fleet touching every namespace

1) Triage: list the distinct namespaces and secret names the Fleet agent SA touched; confirm against the tenant boundary — reads into namespaces owned by a different tenant are the true positive. 2) Contain: rotate the Fleet agent service account token and every secret it read cross-tenant, then apply the patched-version Policy resource pinning a least-privilege service account per GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle namespace. 3) Hunt: correlate back to companion UC (valuesFrom cross-namespace references) to identify which GitRepo/HelmOp/Bundle CR triggered the reads and which tenant Username authored it; upgrade Fleet to v0.15.2/v0.14.6/0.13.11/v0.12.15.

Rancher CVE-2026-44939 exploit URL: authImage YAML injection in /v3/import cluster-import request AIExploitation High
Hunts inbound HTTP requests to the Rancher cluster-import endpoint /v3/import/{token}_{clusterId}.yaml where the authImage query parameter carries URL-encoded newlines or injected YAML keys (command/hostNetwork/securityContext). A well-formed import only ever passes an OCI image reference here, so encoded CR/LF or YAML keywords in authImage are the exploit signature for CVE-2026-44939. Rationale: authImage is documented to accept only an OCI image reference; the presence of %0a/%0d/%250a or YAML keywords (command/hostNetwork/securityContext) inside it on the /v3/import path is the exact CVE-2026-44939 break-out. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory, GitLab Advisory DB and Tenable. Defender left empty: Defender XDR does not ingest web-server access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mhc6-2gfq-xx62 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/rancher/rancher/CVE-2026-44939/ • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-44939
ATT&CKT1190 T1610
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate cluster registration where authImage carries a normal image ref (no encoded newline/YAML keyword) — excluded by the injection-marker clause
  • DAST/vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Nuclei) probing the endpoint with CVE-2026-44939 test payloads
  • Authorized red-team / pentest validating the patch
  • A benign query string that happens to contain the substring 'command' outside authImage (rare on this path)
Response runbook
1) Triage: URL-decode the full authImage value and confirm it contains a newline followed by a YAML key (command:/args:/hostNetwork:). Identify source IP, whether the request returned 200, and which token_clusterId was targeted. 2) Contain: treat the referenced cluster registration token as burned — rotate it and the cattle service-account credentials; block the source IP at the proxy; confirm Rancher is on a patched build (v2.14.2/2.13.6/2.12.10/2.11.14/2.10.12). 3) Hunt: pivot to the downstream cluster's audit log for a kube-api-auth DaemonSet create/modify in cattle-system (UC3) and to endpoints for the matching kubectl apply (UC2).

| where Url contains "%0a" or Url contains "%0d" or Url contains "%250a" or Url contains "command" or Url contains "hostNetwork" or Url contains "securityContext"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, HttpMethod, Url, UserAgent = HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpStatusCode

kubectl apply of malicious Rancher import URL (authImage newline injection) on endpoint AIDelivery High
Hunts kubectl apply invocations pointed at a remote Rancher import manifest whose URL carries the CVE-2026-44939 authImage payload (URL-encoded newlines / injected YAML). This is the victim-operator execution step the advisory describes — applying a maliciously crafted /v3/import URL. Rationale: Ties the article's 'operator runs kubectl apply against a maliciously crafted URL' step to a concrete process event: kubectl + apply + /v3/import/ + authImage. Requiring authImage plus an injection marker keeps this near-zero FP. CloudWatch left empty — endpoint process telemetry, not CloudTrail. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-mhc6-2gfq-xx62 • https://www.tenable.com/cve/CVE-2026-44939
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1610
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Operator applying a legitimate import manifest (authImage is a plain image ref, no %0a/command) — excluded by injection markers
  • CI/CD automation re-registering clusters via kubectl apply of the canonical import URL
  • A security engineer reproducing the CVE in a lab
  • Shell history replay or documentation copy-paste that includes an encoded URL
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "authImage" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "%0a" or ProcessCommandLine contains "%0d" or ProcessCommandLine contains "command")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full command line, URL-decode the authImage value, and confirm an injected YAML key after a newline. Note the user and host that ran kubectl and the target cluster/kubeconfig context. 2) Contain: on the targeted downstream cluster immediately delete/quarantine any kube-api-auth DaemonSet bearing a command:/args: override; rotate the cattle service account and the cluster registration token; isolate the operator workstation if the payload was applied. 3) Hunt: correlate to the inbound exploit request (UC1) and to the resulting DaemonSet create in the cluster audit log (UC3); check for outbound connections from control-plane node pods spawned by the injected command.

| where FileName in~ ("kubectl","kubectl.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "apply"
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "/v3/import/"
| where ProcessCommandLine contains "authImage"

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

Unpatched Argo CD Repo-Server Flaw Could Let Attackers Take Over Kubernetes Clusters

The Hacker News
2026-07-01 12 use cases 4 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Argo CD, a widely used tool for deploying software to Kubernetes, has an unpatched flaw in its repo-server component that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code, provided they can reach the component's internal network port. Synacktiv, which found the bug, says it can lead to a full cluster takeover. There is no fix and no CVE. The firm says it reported the flaw to Argo CD's maintainers in

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).

Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Argo CD repo-server spawns shell/network tool or abuses kustomize --helm-command · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Unexpected read of Argo CD namespace secrets by non-Argo-CD principal · [LLM] Argo CD-linked RBAC privilege escalation (cluster-admin binding) · [LLM] NetworkPolicy deleted in Argo CD namespace (containment disabled) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Argo CD repo-server spawns shell/network tool or abuses kustomize --helm-command AIExploitation High
Hunts the core Synacktiv RCE: the argocd-repo-server (via kustomize) is coerced into running an attacker script instead of helm by setting kustomize's --helm-command to a non-helm path pulled from a malicious Git repo. Surfaces argocd-repo-server/kustomize/helm spawning shells or net tools, and any --helm-command argument that does not resolve to a helm binary. Rationale: Uses the exact abused flag named in the article and confirmed by Synacktiv (--helm-command / --enable-helm) plus the specific Argo CD binary chain (argocd-repo-server -> kustomize -> helm). repo-server spawning a shell/curl/wget is anomalous because it only legitimately runs git/helm/kustomize; the regex filters the legitimate --helm-command <path>/helm usage. Cross-checked Synacktiv 'Caught in the Octopus Trap' advisory. Cross-checked against: • https://www.synacktiv.com/en/publications/caught-in-the-octopus-trap-unauthenticated-rce-in-argo-cd-with-codeql • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4192188/argo-cd-flaw-shows-why-gitops-infrastructure-should-be-treated-as-tier-zero.html
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom Config Management Plugins (CMPs) that legitimately shell out from repo-server (e.g. jsonnet/ytt wrappers invoking bash)
  • Helm hooks or kustomize exec plugins run by platform teams that call curl/wget to fetch charts
  • repo-server init containers or debugging (kubectl exec into repo-server for troubleshooting)
  • Legitimate --helm-command pointing to a wrapper script literally named helm (excluded by regex but variant naming could slip)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("cmp-server","config-management-plugin","/plugins/"))
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: Pull the full ChildCmd and ParentCmd; confirm the process ran inside an argocd-repo-server pod and whether --helm-command references a path outside the helm binary (e.g. /tmp git-checkout dir or a .sh). Check if a Config Management Plugin is configured that would explain a shell child. Step 2 - Contain: Cordon/isolate the node, delete the repo-server pod, and immediately apply Argo CD's NetworkPolicies (set networkPolicy.create=true) so only Argo CD components can reach repo-server:8081 and Redis:6379. Rotate REDIS_PASSWORD. Step 3 - Hunt: Pivot on the same host for outbound connections to Redis 6379, egress to attacker Git/registry hosts, and subsequent privileged workload deploys by argocd-application-controller (see related UCs).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize","helm")
| where (FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","ruby","socat")) or (ProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command")
| where not(ProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command" and ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)--helm-command\s+\S*helm($|\s)")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ParentImage=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ChildImage=FolderPath, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("argocd-repo-server","kustomize","helm")
| where (TargetProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl","ruby","socat")) or (TargetProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command")
| where not(TargetProcessCommandLine has "--helm-command" and TargetProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)--helm-command\s+\S*helm($|\s)")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Unexpected read of Argo CD namespace secrets by non-Argo-CD principal AIActions on Objectives Medium
Post-RCE the attacker reads cluster/repo credentials from the argocd namespace (article cites CVE-2025-55190 repo-cred theft and CVE-2026-42880 plaintext-secret reads). Flags get/list/watch on secrets in the argocd namespace by any identity that is NOT an Argo CD service account or the kubelet, catching credential enumeration via a compromised token or pod. Rationale: Grounds on the article's named secret-exposure CVEs (CVE-2025-55190 repo credential leak, CVE-2026-42880 plaintext secret read) plus the demonstrated REDIS_PASSWORD theft. The argocd namespace + secrets resource is the exact credential store; excluding Argo CD's own service accounts and the kubelet removes the legitimate readers, leaving anomalous enumeration. No Defender/Falcon query as K8s API audit is not in FDR/MDE tables. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://www.synacktiv.com/en/publications/caught-in-the-octopus-trap-unauthenticated-rce-in-argo-cd-with-codeql
ATT&CKT1552.007 T1555.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Platform engineers using kubectl to inspect Argo CD repo/cluster secrets during troubleshooting
  • Backup tooling (Velero) enumerating secrets in argocd for cluster backups
  • GitOps CI service accounts from another namespace legitimately reading a shared repo-credential secret
  • Monitoring/compliance scanners (kube-bench, Trivy operator) listing secrets cluster-wide
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "velero" and UserAgent !has "trivy" and UserAgent !has "kube-bench"
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: Identify the Username/UserAgent and source of the read; determine if it is a human kubectl session, a known backup/scanner tool, or an unexpected serviceaccount/pod token. Enumerate which SecretNames were read (repo-creds, cluster secrets, redis secret). Step 2 - Contain: If unauthorized, revoke the token/rotate the serviceaccount, and rotate every credential in the accessed secrets (Git repo creds, cluster kubeconfigs, REDIS_PASSWORD). Enable Argo CD NetworkPolicies. Step 3 - Hunt: Correlate the reader identity with prior repo-server shell activity (UC1), Redis 6379 connections, and any new Applications/RBAC bindings created shortly after the secret read.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| where Verb in ("get","list","watch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "secrets" and tostring(ObjectRef.namespace) == "argocd"
| where Username !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:"
| where Username !startswith "system:node:"
| where Username != "system:apiserver"
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, SecretName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| stats count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values("objectRef.name") as secrets values(sourceIPs{}) as srcIPs by "user.username" userAgent
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Argo CD application-controller deploys privileged / host-namespace workload AIInstallation High
After poisoning Argo CD's Redis cache, the next sync makes Argo CD deploy the attacker's workload. This flags the Argo CD application-controller service account creating pods/workloads with privileged=true, hostPID/hostNetwork, or a /var/run/docker.sock hostPath mount — the classic container-breakout payload delivered through GitOps. Rationale: Grounds on the article's stated outcome: 'On the next automatic sync, Argo CD deployed an attacker-supplied workload' (corroborated by Cycode CVE-2024-31989 write-up). The Argo CD application-controller service account is the only expected deployer, so a privileged/hostPID/hostNetwork/docker.sock spec from it is high-fidelity breakout payload delivery. K8s audit only; not present in FDR/MDE tables. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://cycode.com/blog/revealing-argo-cd-critical-vulnerability/ • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-9766-5277-j5hr
ATT&CKT1610 T1072
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimately GitOps-managed privileged DaemonSets (CNI plugins, node-exporter, Falco, storage CSI drivers) synced by Argo CD
  • Platform teams onboarding a monitoring agent that mounts hostPath for logs
  • Ingress controllers using hostNetwork:true by design
  • A newly added, approved privileged workload during a maintenance window
Suppression filter
| where Namespace !in ("kube-system","monitoring","falco","ingress-nginx")
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: Diff the workload's owning Argo CD Application and its source Git repo/commit — is this manifest present in the intended repo history, or did it appear only in the live cluster (cache-poisoning drift)? Check the image registry and the securityContext. Step 2 - Contain: Delete the offending workload, pause the parent Application auto-sync, and rotate REDIS_PASSWORD (the cache is unsigned, so the poison must be evicted). Flush the poisoned Redis 'mfst' cache entries. Step 3 - Hunt: Look for the preceding repo-server shell exec (UC1), Redis 6379 connections from repo-server, and any RBAC bindings the new pod's service account was granted (UC4).
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where Username startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:"
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) in ("pods","deployments","daemonsets","statefulsets","replicasets")
| extend body = tostring(RequestObject)
| where body contains '"privileged":true' or body contains '"hostPID":true' or body contains '"hostNetwork":true' or body contains 'docker.sock'
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), Name = tostring(ObjectRef.name), Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Argo CD Controller Deploys Privileged or Host-Namespace Workload
id: 5c1e7a92-4f88-4b13-9d0a-6e2b4c9f8a11
status: experimental
description: Detects the Argo CD application-controller creating pods/workloads with privileged containers, host PID/network, or a docker.sock hostPath mount, consistent with a poisoned-cache attacker workload deployed on sync.

source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @user.username:system\:serviceaccount\:argocd\:* @objectRef.resource:(pods OR deployments OR daemonsets OR statefulsets) (@requestObject.spec.containers.securityContext.privileged:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostPID:true OR @requestObject.spec.hostNetwork:true OR @requestObject.spec.volumes.hostPath.path:*docker.sock*)
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" stage=ResponseComplete verb IN ("create","update","patch") "user.username"="system:serviceaccount:argocd:*" "objectRef.resource" IN ("pods","deployments","daemonsets","statefulsets","replicasets")
| search _raw="*\"privileged\":true*" OR _raw="*\"hostPID\":true*" OR _raw="*\"hostNetwork\":true*" OR _raw="*docker.sock*"
| table _time "user.username" verb "objectRef.resource" "objectRef.name" "objectRef.namespace"
Argo CD-linked RBAC privilege escalation (cluster-admin binding) AIActions on Objectives High
Full cluster takeover requires elevating Argo CD's foothold. This flags creation/modification of ClusterRoleBindings/RoleBindings that either grant cluster-admin or bind an argocd-namespace service account, indicating an attacker widening permissions after repo-server compromise. Rationale: Grounds on the article's central claim that the flaw 'can lead to a full cluster takeover' — takeover requires elevated RBAC. Binding cluster-admin or granting an argocd service account new cluster-scoped rights is the concrete escalation event. String-anchored on the exact roleRef 'cluster-admin' and the argocd namespace subject. K8s audit only. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://www.csoonline.com/article/4192188/argo-cd-flaw-shows-why-gitops-infrastructure-should-be-treated-as-tier-zero.html
ATT&CKT1098 T1548
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Argo CD install/upgrade (Helm/Argo CD operator) legitimately creating its own cluster-admin or application-controller ClusterRoleBinding
  • Platform IaC (Terraform/Flux) reconciling RBAC that references cluster-admin
  • A new managed add-on's bootstrap job granting itself broad rights
  • Break-glass admin manually binding cluster-admin during incident response
Suppression filter
| where BindingName !startswith "argocd-" and Username !has "helm" and Username !has "terraform"
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: Identify the creating Username and whether it is a Helm/operator install context vs an unexpected identity; inspect the binding's subjects and roleRef. Determine what the bound principal can now do. Step 2 - Contain: If unauthorized, delete the RoleBinding/ClusterRoleBinding, revoke the subject's tokens, and audit for resources already created under the elevated rights. Step 3 - Hunt: Correlate the creator identity with prior repo-server RCE (UC1), argocd secret reads (UC2), and any privileged workloads it subsequently deployed (UC3).
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings")
| extend body = tostring(RequestObject)
| where body contains "cluster-admin" or (body contains '"kind":"ServiceAccount"' and body contains '"namespace":"argocd"')
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, BindingName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), Namespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), RequestBody = body
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Argo CD-Linked RBAC Privilege Escalation Binding

Argo CD Application/ApplicationSet pointed at first-seen external Git repo AIInstallation Medium
Persistence through GitOps: the attacker creates/edits an Argo CD Application or ApplicationSet whose source repoURL points to an attacker-controlled Git repository never previously seen in the cluster. Uses a 30-day baseline of known repoURLs and alerts on any newly introduced source repo. Rationale: Grounds on the article/reviewer premise that takeover is sustained by deploying attacker-controlled workloads from an attacker Git repo. The Application CRD's spec.source.repoURL is the exact GitOps injection point; a first-seen repoURL (30-day baseline leftanti) surfaces the new attacker source without hardcoding the org's repos. Datadog carries the filter only; new-value detection on repoURL is set at rule level (no in-query baseline). Sigma skipped (requires baseline/anti-join). Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://www.synacktiv.com/en/publications/caught-in-the-octopus-trap-unauthenticated-rce-in-argo-cd-with-codeql
ATT&CKT1525 T1072
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate onboarding of a new microservice repo into GitOps
  • Team migrating repos to a new Git host (GitHub -> GitLab) creating new repoURLs
  • App-of-apps pattern generating child Applications with new source paths
  • Dev/staging Applications referencing short-lived feature-branch repos
Suppression filter
| where repo has_any ("github.com","gitlab.com","dev.azure.com","bitbucket.org") == false
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: Resolve the new repoURL — is it an approved internal Git host or an external/attacker-controlled domain? Confirm the creating Username is an expected GitOps operator and the change appears in a legitimate PR. Step 2 - Contain: If malicious, delete/revert the Application, pause auto-sync, and block egress to the external Git host. Rotate REDIS_PASSWORD and repo credentials. Step 3 - Hunt: Enumerate all Applications from that repoURL, inspect their rendered manifests for privileged/host-namespace workloads (UC3), and trace the creator identity back to repo-server RCE or secret access (UC1/UC2).
let Baseline = AKSAudit
    | where TimeGenerated between (ago(30d) .. ago(1d))
    | where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) in ("applications","applicationsets")
    | extend repo = tostring(RequestObject.spec.source.repoURL)
    | where isnotempty(repo)
    | distinct repo;
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) in ("applications","applicationsets")
| extend repo = tostring(RequestObject.spec.source.repoURL)
| where isnotempty(repo)
| join kind=leftanti Baseline on repo
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, AppName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), repo
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update OR patch) @objectRef.resource:(applications OR applicationsets)
CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" verb IN ("create","update","patch") "objectRef.resource" IN ("applications","applicationsets")
| spath output=repo path=requestObject.spec.source.repoURL
| where isnotnull(repo)
| eventstats earliest(_time) as first_seen by repo
| where first_seen > relative_time(now(), "-1d@d")
| table _time "user.username" verb "objectRef.name" repo
| sort - _time
NetworkPolicy deleted in Argo CD namespace (containment disabled) AIActions on Objectives Medium
The article's only real defense is Kubernetes NetworkPolicies isolating repo-server and Redis. This flags deletion of a networkpolicy in the argocd namespace by a non-Argo-CD identity — an attacker removing the wall so a compromised pod can reach repo-server:8081 and Redis:6379. Rationale: Directly grounds on the article's mitigation guidance ('Turn on Kubernetes network policies so only Argo CD's own components can reach the repo-server and Redis ports' / 'kubectl get networkpolicy -A'). Deleting a networkpolicy in the argocd namespace is the inverse action an attacker takes to enable exploitation, anchored on the exact resource and namespace. K8s audit only. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/unpatched-argo-cd-repo-server-flaw.html • https://howtofix.guide/argo-cd-repo-server-rce-networkpolicy/
ATT&CKT1562.007
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Platform team refactoring/renaming NetworkPolicies during an Argo CD upgrade
  • Helm/IaC reconcile that deletes-and-recreates a policy on chart value change
  • Cluster admin temporarily removing a policy to debug connectivity
  • Migration from Calico to Cilium network policies replacing existing objects
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !has "helm" and UserAgent !has "argocd-application-controller"
Response runbook
Step 1 - Triage: Confirm the deleting Username and whether a matching recreate event follows within seconds (Helm delete-then-create is benign). Check if any repo-server/Redis-reaching connections occurred in the window the policy was absent. Step 2 - Contain: Immediately re-apply Argo CD's provided NetworkPolicies (networkPolicy.create=true) restoring isolation on repo-server:8081 and Redis:6379; if the deleter is unauthorized, revoke its token. Step 3 - Hunt: Search for pods that connected to repo-server or Redis while the policy was down, and for the exploitation chain (UC1 repo-server shell, UC3 privileged deploy) during that gap.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Stage == "ResponseComplete"
| where Verb == "delete"
| where tostring(ObjectRef.resource) == "networkpolicies" and tostring(ObjectRef.namespace) == "argocd"
| where Username !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:"
| project TimeGenerated, Username, Verb, PolicyName = tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

ImFileEvent

| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")

status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02

    - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:

            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Entra help-desk MFA/password reset followed by sign-in from new IP (Scattered Spider ATO) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha)
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] External/guest identity active in Teams during breach response (Scattered Spider watching defenders) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Entra help-desk MFA/password reset followed by sign-in from new IP (Scattered Spider ATO) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts Scattered Spider's signature account-takeover: an IT-help-desk-driven credential or MFA-method reset immediately followed by a successful sign-in for that same user from a different IP within one hour. Article-specific because the body explicitly states the group phones help desks to 'reset a password or approve a login' — this correlates the reset event to the first attacker login. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit claim that Scattered Spider convinces help desks to 'reset a password or approve a login'; correlates the Entra/AD reset event to the first successful sign-in from a different IP within 1h — the actual ATO moment. Cross-checked against CISA AA23-320A which documents help-desk MFA-method reset (T1556.006). Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://www.ic3.gov/CSA/2025/250729.pdf • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1556.006 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate help-desk password reset when a genuinely-locked-out employee then signs in from home (different IP than the help-desk agent)
  • User travels and legitimately re-registers MFA from a new location after losing a device
  • VPN/proxy egress causes the post-reset sign-in IP to differ from the reset-request IP for the same real user
  • Bulk password-reset campaigns after an org-wide forced credential rotation
  • Self-service password reset from a mobile network (carrier IP) immediately followed by desktop sign-in
Suppression filter
| where DeviceTrustType != "Compliant" and Country != "<user home country>"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the reset event's InitiatedBy — was it a help-desk/admin account or true self-service? Compare ResetIP vs FirstSignInIP geolocation/ASN and check if the sign-in device is compliant/known. Contact the user out-of-band (not via Teams/chat) to confirm they requested the reset. 2) Contain: if unconfirmed, revoke all refresh tokens (Revoke-MgUserSignInSession), disable the account, and force a re-registration of MFA under IT supervision. 3) Hunt: review the same account's sign-ins, mailbox-rule creation, OAuth app consents, and Teams/chat joins in the following 24h; check whether the help-desk agent handled other suspicious resets in the same shift.
let win = 1h;
let resets = IdentityDirectoryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Account Password reset","Account Password changed")
| project ResetTime = Timestamp, TargetUpn = AccountUpn, ResetActor = AccountName, ResetDetail = tostring(AdditionalFields)
| where isnotempty(TargetUpn);
resets
| join kind=inner (
    AADSignInEventsBeta
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ErrorCode == 0
    | project SignInTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Country, City, Application, DeviceTrustType
) on $left.TargetUpn == $right.AccountUpn
| where SignInTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + win)
| summarize arg_min(SignInTime, *), FirstSignInIP = any(IPAddress) by TargetUpn, ResetTime
| extend DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ResetTime)
| project ResetTime, SignInTime, DelayMin, TargetUpn, ResetActor, FirstSignInIP, Country, City, Application, DeviceTrustType
| order by ResetTime desc
let win = 1h;
let resets = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where LoggedByService in ("Authentication Methods","Core Directory","Self-service Password Management","Account Provisioning")
| where ActivityDisplayName has_any ("Reset user password","Reset password (by admin)","Admin registered security info","User registered security info","Admin updated security info","User started security info registration")
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| extend InitiatedByUpn = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| extend ResetIP = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| where isnotempty(TargetUpn)
| project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, ActivityDisplayName, TargetUpn, InitiatedByUpn, ResetIP;
resets
| join kind=inner (
    SigninLogs
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ResultType == 0
    | project SignInTime = TimeGenerated, UserPrincipalName, SignInIP = IPAddress, AppDisplayName, Location
) on $left.TargetUpn == $right.UserPrincipalName
| where SignInTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + win)
| where SignInIP != ResetIP
| summarize arg_min(SignInTime, *) by TargetUpn, ResetTime
| extend DelayMin = datetime_diff('minute', SignInTime, ResetTime)
| project ResetTime, SignInTime, DelayMin, TargetUpn, ActivityDisplayName, InitiatedByUpn, ResetIP, SignInIP, AppDisplayName, Location
| order by ResetTime desc

External/guest identity active in Teams during breach response (Scattered Spider watching defenders) AIActions on Objectives Low
Hunts the joint-advisory behaviour the article calls out: once inside, Scattered Spider 'lurk in a company's chat tools and join the calls it holds to respond to the breach.' Surfaces guest/external (#EXT#) identities joining Teams meetings, being added to teams/chats, or reading messages — a signal an intruder is monitoring the incident-response effort. Rationale: Directly implements the article's quoted advisory line about intruders joining the breach-response calls/chat; pivots on guest/#EXT# identity performing Teams meeting-join and message-read operations, which is not covered by generic phishing/exec rules. Corroborated by CISA AA23-320A on Scattered Spider persistence in collaboration tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1015/
ATT&CKT1213.005 T1078.004
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: high — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate external partners/MSSP/DFIR retainer consultants invited into the actual incident-response bridge (expected guests)
  • Vendor or auditor guest accounts routinely joining recurring cross-org meetings
  • Contractors with B2B guest access participating in normal project chats
  • New guest onboarding during M&A or partner integration generating MemberAdded events
  • External Teams federation for legitimate customer-support conversations
Suppression filter
| where UserId !has_any ("@trusted-mssp.com","@dfir-retainer.com")
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each guest identity, verify the invitation provenance — who added them (check the corresponding AuditLogs 'Add member to group'/'Invite external user' event), when the guest tenant/domain was first seen, and whether it aligns with a sanctioned partner. Prioritize guests added AFTER the breach-response channel was created. 2) Contain: if unrecognized, remove the guest from all teams/meetings, block the external domain in Teams federation/guest-access policy, and move IR coordination to an out-of-band channel the attacker cannot see. 3) Hunt: correlate the guest's AccountId/IP with SigninLogs and the reset-correlation detection above; review what channels/files the guest accessed and whether the same external domain appears in OAuth consents or mailbox forwarding.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType in ("MemberAdded","TeamsSessionStarted","MeetingParticipantDetail","MessagesListed","ChatCreated","MessageSent")
| extend RawUpn = tostring(RawEventData.UserId)
| where AccountType == "Guest" or RawUpn has "#EXT#" or AccountDisplayName has "#EXT#"
| project Timestamp, ActionType, AccountDisplayName, AccountId, AccountType, RawUpn, IPAddress, CountryCode, City, ObjectName
| order by Timestamp desc
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in ("MemberAdded","TeamsSessionStarted","MeetingParticipantDetail","MeetingDetail","MessagesListed","ChatCreated","MessageSent","MemberRoleChanged")
| where ExternalAccess == true or UserType == "Guest" or UserId has "#EXT#"
| project TimeGenerated, Operation, UserId, UserType, ExternalAccess, ClientIP, UserAgent, ObjectId
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId

SecurityEvent

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
